Ramadan. The ninth month of the Islamic calendar, observed by Muslims worldwide as a period of fasting, prayer, and spiritual reflection. During daylight hours, Muslims abstain from food, water, and other worldly indulgences as an act of devotion and self-discipline. It commemorates the revelation of the Quran to the Prophet Muhammad and is one of the Five Pillars of Islam.

Ramadan is determined by the lunar calendar, so it shifts roughly eleven days earlier each solar year. The same month cycles through all seasons over thirty-three years.

The fast, called sawm, requires abstention from dawn to sunset. Sick, elderly, pregnant, and menstruating individuals are exempted and may fast at another time. The pre-dawn meal is called suhoor. Breaking the fast is called iftar, and the iftar is often a communal celebration, reinforcing bonds within Muslim families and communities.

Taraweeh prayers, special evening prayers, are performed throughout Ramadan, often reading through the entire Quran over the month.

The Night of Power, Laylat al-Qadr, falls in the last ten nights of Ramadan and is believed to be when the Quran was first revealed. Worship this night is considered especially meritorious.

Ramadan emphasizes empathy for the poor and hungry. Muslims are encouraged to give zakat, alms, and perform acts of charity.

The month concludes with Eid al-Fitr, a joyous festival and public holiday in Muslim-majority countries, marked by prayers, feasting, and gift-giving.
